gloss: A very large sea mammal that breathes air through a hole on top of its head.
examples: We saw a *whale* breach about a hundred yards off the boat.
*Whales* migrate down this coast every winter.
The museum has a life-size blue *whale* hanging from the ceiling.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *wail* (to cry loudly).

gloss: A smart, playful sea mammal with a long snout.
examples: A pair of *dolphins* followed the ferry for almost a mile.
My daughter wants to swim with *dolphins* on our trip.
A *dolphin* is a mammal, not a fish.

gloss: A small sea mammal like a dolphin but shorter, with a blunt nose.
examples: *Porpoises* are stockier than dolphins and have blunter faces.
We spotted a *porpoise* in the bay at dawn.
The crew pulled in the nets to avoid catching a *porpoise*.
contrast: The ending is said like the word *purpose*, not 'poyz'.

gloss: A sea mammal with short flippers that comes ashore to rest.
examples: A *seal* was sunning itself on the rocks below the trail.
The far end of the dock is crowded with *seals*.
We watched a baby *seal* learn to swim.

gloss: A large seal with visible ear flaps that can walk on its front flippers.
examples: The *sea lions* down at the pier are a tourist attraction.
A *sea lion* can move surprisingly fast on land.
You can hear the *sea lions* barking from three blocks away.

gloss: A huge Arctic sea mammal with two long tusks and thick whiskers.
examples: A full-grown *walrus* can weigh more than a ton.
The zoo's new exhibit has two *walruses*.
He grew a mustache that made him look like a *walrus*.

gloss: A small furry water animal with webbed feet and a long tail.
examples: A sea *otter* floated on its back cracking open a clam.
*Otters* hold hands so they don't drift apart while they sleep.
An *otter* slid down the muddy bank and disappeared.

gloss: A slow, heavy plant-eating sea mammal of warm shallow water.
examples: *Manatees* gather in the warm water near the power plant.
A *manatee* can eat a tenth of its body weight in a day.
We rented kayaks and paddled out to see the *manatees*.

gloss: A large black-and-white whale that hunts in family groups.
examples: An *orca* surfaced right next to the kayak.
*Orcas* hunt together and teach their young how to do it.
The park stopped keeping *orcas* years ago.

gloss: An Arctic whale whose long straight tusk sticks out from its head.
examples: A *narwhal*'s tusk is really one giant tooth.
*Narwhals* live under the Arctic ice year-round.
Sailors used to sell *narwhal* tusks as unicorn horns.
contrast: The *h* is silent: NAR-wahl.

gloss: A large fish with rows of sharp teeth and a fin that shows above the water.
examples: They closed the beach after someone spotted a *shark*.
Most *sharks* have no interest in people at all.
The aquarium's tunnel takes you right under the *sharks*.

gloss: A soft, clear sea animal with trailing tentacles that can sting.
examples: A *jellyfish* stung my ankle in the shallow water.
There were hundreds of *jellyfish* washed up on the sand.
Don't touch that *jellyfish*, even if it looks dead.
contrast: The plural is usually *jellyfish*, unchanged — not 'jellyfishes'.

gloss: A flat sea animal shaped like a star, usually with five arms.
examples: My son found a purple *starfish* stuck to a rock.
A *starfish* can grow a new arm if it loses one.
The tide left a dozen *starfish* behind on the sand.
contrast: The plural is normally *starfish*, unchanged.

gloss: Another name for a starfish, now preferred by scientists.
examples: Biologists say *sea star* because the animal isn't a fish.
A disease wiped out millions of *sea stars* along this coast.
We counted six *sea stars* in one tide pool.

gloss: A small round sea animal covered in sharp spines.
examples: I stepped on a *sea urchin* and limped for a week.
*Sea urchins* eat kelp right down to the rock.
The chef served *sea urchin* on toast.

gloss: A soft sea animal that sits on a rock and waves stinging tentacles like petals.
examples: A *sea anemone* closed up when I touched the water.
Clownfish live safely among the *sea anemones*.
The tide pool was lined with green *sea anemones*.
contrast: Four syllables in *anemone*: uh-NEM-uh-nee.

gloss: A long soft sea animal that crawls along the bottom eating scraps.
examples: A *sea cucumber* was inching across the sand.
*Sea cucumbers* are a delicacy in parts of Asia.
The diver picked up a *sea cucumber* and put it right back.

gloss: A small shell-less sea animal, often brightly colored.
examples: The photo showed a *sea slug* in electric blue and orange.
*Sea slugs* have some of the strangest colors in the ocean.
He spent the whole dive looking for one *sea slug*.

gloss: A squid-like sea animal that can change color in seconds.
examples: A *cuttlefish* flashed from brown to white as we watched.
*Cuttlefish* are considered among the smartest invertebrates.
The pet store sells *cuttlefish* bone for birds.
contrast: The plural is usually *cuttlefish*, unchanged.

gloss: A small freshwater animal like a tiny lobster, with claws and a hard shell.
examples: We caught *crayfish* in the creek with a net and a piece of bacon.
A pound of boiled *crayfish* costs almost nothing down there.
A *crayfish* backed into a hole under the rock.
contrast: In much of the South it's *crawfish* or *crawdad* — same animal.

gloss: A small hard-shelled sea creature that fastens itself to rocks and boats.
examples: The hull was crusted with *barnacles*.
A *barnacle* glues itself down for life.
They scraped the *barnacles* off before repainting the boat.

gloss: A large spiral sea shell, or the sea snail that lives in it.
examples: He blew into a *conch* like a horn.
*Conch* fritters are on every menu in the Keys.
She keeps a pink *conch* on the windowsill.
contrast: Said 'konk' — the *ch* is /k/, not 'ch'.

gloss: A sea snail with a flat ear-shaped shell that shines inside.
examples: Divers used to pull *abalone* off these rocks by the sackful.
An *abalone* shell makes a beautiful ashtray.
*Abalone* is expensive because it's been overharvested.
contrast: The final *e* is pronounced: ab-uh-LOH-nee, four syllables.

gloss: A deep-sea animal that lives in a coiled shell divided into chambers.
examples: A cut-open *nautilus* shell shows a perfect spiral.
*Nautiluses* have barely changed in millions of years.
The gift shop sells a polished *nautilus* for forty dollars.

gloss: A soft-bodied crab that lives inside an empty shell it carries around.
examples: A *hermit crab* scuttled across the tide pool.
*Hermit crabs* trade shells as they outgrow them.
My daughter kept a *hermit crab* in a tank for two years.

gloss: A blue-clawed crab of the Atlantic coast, caught for its meat.
examples: We steamed a bushel of *blue crabs* on the back porch.
The *blue crab* season runs through the fall.
Maryland is famous for *blue crab*.

gloss: A very large cold-water crab with long spiny legs, sold for its meat.
examples: *King crab* legs are the most expensive thing on the menu.
A single *king crab* can weigh close to twenty pounds.
The boat came back loaded with *king crabs*.

gloss: An ancient armored sea animal with a rounded shell and a spike-like tail.
examples: Thousands of *horseshoe crabs* come ashore to spawn each spring.
A *horseshoe crab* isn't really a crab at all.
Their blue blood makes *horseshoe crabs* valuable to medicine.

gloss: A flat round sea creature whose white skeleton washes up on beaches.
examples: I found a whole *sand dollar* without a single crack.
*Sand dollars* bleach white once they dry out.
Leave a live *sand dollar* where you found it.

gloss: An animal with a hard outer shell and jointed legs, such as a crab or shrimp.
examples: Lobsters, crabs, and shrimp are all *crustaceans*.
She's allergic to every *crustacean* there is.
The reef supports dozens of *crustacean* species.
contrast: The *ce* is said /ʃ/: kruh-STAY-shun.

gloss: A soft-bodied animal that usually has a shell, such as a clam or a snail.
examples: Oysters and squid are both *mollusks*.
A *mollusk* builds its shell out of the minerals in seawater.
The class spent a week on *mollusks*.
contrast: American spelling *mollusk*; British *mollusc*.

gloss: A flat fish that glides along the bottom and has a stinging spine on its tail.
examples: A *stingray* slid out from under the sand right by my foot.
Shuffle your feet so you don't step on a *stingray*.
*Stingrays* only sting when they feel trapped.

gloss: A huge harmless ray with wide triangular fins that seems to fly underwater.
examples: A *manta ray* passed right over the divers.
*Manta rays* can be twenty feet across.
Seeing a *manta ray* was the best part of the trip.

gloss: A flat diamond-shaped fish related to rays, with no stinging tail.
examples: The fish market had *skate* wing on ice.
A *skate* buried itself until only its eyes showed.
*Skate* tastes a little like scallops.
contrast: Spelled and said like the ice *skate* — only context tells them apart.

gloss: A shark whose head sticks out sideways with an eye at each end.
examples: A *hammerhead* cruised past the drop-off.
*Hammerheads* gather here by the hundreds in summer.
You can identify a *hammerhead* from a long way off.

gloss: A very large gray-and-white shark known for attacking seals near shore.
examples: Tagged *great white sharks* pass this beach every fall.
The movie made everyone afraid of the *great white shark*.
A *great white shark* can grow past sixteen feet.

gloss: The largest fish in the world, a spotted shark that eats tiny plankton.
examples: We snorkeled next to a *whale shark* for twenty minutes.
*Whale sharks* are completely harmless to people.
Each *whale shark* has its own pattern of spots.

gloss: A long silver fish with a jutting jaw full of teeth.
examples: A *barracuda* hung in the water watching us.
*Barracudas* are drawn to anything shiny.
He hooked a four-foot *barracuda* off the reef.

gloss: A big ocean game fish with a long pointed bill and a tall fin.
examples: He fought a blue *marlin* for three hours.
*Marlin* are almost always released these days.
There's a mounted *marlin* over the bar.
contrast: The plural is usually *marlin*, unchanged.

gloss: A thick snake-like fish that lives in reef holes with its mouth open.
examples: A *moray eel* poked its head out of the coral.
*Moray eels* look mean but mostly leave divers alone.
Don't put your hand in a hole — that's where the *moray eels* are.
contrast: *Moray* is said MOR-ay, with the stress on the first syllable.

gloss: Any of several ocean food fish with firm white flesh.
examples: I ordered the grilled *sea bass*.
They pulled in two big *sea bass* before noon.
Chilean *sea bass* got so popular it was nearly fished out.
contrast: *Bass* the fish rhymes with *class* /bæs/; *bass* the low sound is /beɪs/.

gloss: A large, long-lived bony fish whose eggs are sold as caviar.
examples: A *sturgeon* jumped clear out of the river.
*Sturgeon* can live for over a century.
Smoked *sturgeon* is a deli staple in New York.

gloss: A cheap white ocean fish used in fish sticks and fast-food sandwiches.
examples: Most frozen fish sticks are made from *pollock*.
The fleet brought in tons of *pollock*.
*Pollock* is milder than cod and costs less.

gloss: A silvery coastal fish that travels in schools and often jumps.
examples: A school of *mullet* boiled up right off the beach.
Smoked *mullet* is a Florida tradition.
He threw a cast net and came up with a dozen *mullet*.
contrast: The same word also names the haircut — only context tells you which.

gloss: A fast ocean fish with a bill and a tall fin like a sail on its back.
examples: A *sailfish* is said to be the fastest fish in the ocean.
He released the *sailfish* after a quick photo.
*Sailfish* raise that fin when they're excited.

gloss: A tiny upright fish with a curled tail and a head shaped like a horse's.
examples: A *seahorse* was holding onto a blade of seagrass.
In *seahorses*, the male carries the eggs.
The tank had two *seahorses* and nothing else.

gloss: A venomous snake that lives in warm ocean water and has a flat paddle tail.
examples: A *sea snake* swam past the boat.
*Sea snakes* have to surface to breathe.
There are no *sea snakes* in the Atlantic.

gloss: A small orange-and-white reef fish that shelters in a sea anemone.
examples: Every kid can recognize a *clownfish* now.
*Clownfish* never stray far from their anemone.
We added a *clownfish* to the saltwater tank.

gloss: A tall, flat, brightly colored reef fish.
examples: A yellow *angelfish* drifted along the coral.
*Angelfish* are popular with aquarium keepers.
That *angelfish* has been in the tank for years.

gloss: A fish that blows itself up into a spiny ball when it is threatened.
examples: The *pufferfish* doubled in size in about a second.
Some *pufferfish* are poisonous enough to kill a person.
He photographed a *pufferfish* hiding under a ledge.

gloss: A striped reef fish with long venomous spines, now a pest in the Atlantic.
examples: *Lionfish* have taken over parts of the Caribbean.
Divers are paid to spear every *lionfish* they see.
A *lionfish* sting is extremely painful.

gloss: A colorful reef fish with a beak-like mouth that scrapes algae off coral.
examples: You can hear a *parrotfish* crunching on the reef.
Much of this white sand came out of *parrotfish*.
A blue *parrotfish* swam by twice.

gloss: A small orange fish commonly kept as a pet.
examples: He won a *goldfish* at the fair.
Both *goldfish* died over the weekend.
A *goldfish* needs more room than a bowl.
contrast: The plural is *goldfish*, unchanged — not 'goldfishes'.

gloss: Any very small fish, often used as live bait.
examples: A cloud of *minnows* scattered when my shadow hit the water.
We stopped for a bucket of *minnows* on the way out.
He hooked a live *minnow* through the lip.

gloss: The everyday name for the orca, a large black-and-white hunting whale.
examples: A pod of *killer whales* went by just after sunrise.
The *killer whale* is really the largest dolphin.
*Killer whales* have their own dialects.

gloss: The largest animal that has ever lived, a huge gray-blue baleen whale.
examples: A *blue whale*'s heart is the size of a small car.
*Blue whales* feed almost entirely on krill.
We were lucky enough to see a *blue whale* off Monterey.

gloss: A large whale with long white flippers, known for leaping and for singing.
examples: A *humpback whale* breached twice right beside us.
*Humpback whales* sing songs that last for hours.
The *humpback whale* population has recovered a lot.

gloss: A deep-diving whale with a huge square head that hunts giant squid.
examples: A *sperm whale* can dive over a mile down.
Whalers once hunted *sperm whales* for lamp oil.
*Moby-Dick* is about a white *sperm whale*.

gloss: A mottled gray whale that migrates along the Pacific coast every year.
examples: *Gray whales* pass this headland from December to February.
A mother *gray whale* stayed close to her calf.
The *gray whale* migration is one of the longest of any mammal.
contrast: American spelling *gray whale*; British *grey whale*.

gloss: A small white Arctic whale with a rounded forehead and no back fin.
examples: A *beluga* swam up to the glass and stared at the kids.
*Belugas* are so chatty they're called sea canaries.
The *beluga* turns white only as an adult.
contrast: In English *beluga* also names the sturgeon that beluga caviar comes from.

gloss: A thin flat part on a fish's body that it uses to steer and swim.
examples: A *fin* cut through the water about fifty feet out.
The fish beat its *fins* and shot under the dock.
He grabbed it carefully to avoid the sharp *fin*.

gloss: The fin on the back of a fish or whale, the one you see above the water.
examples: You can tell orcas apart by their *dorsal fins*.
A tall *dorsal fin* broke the surface.
The *dorsal fin* on that male is almost six feet high.

gloss: One of the organs a fish uses to take oxygen out of water.
examples: Fish breathe through their *gills*.
You can judge how fresh a fish is by the color of its *gills*.
A single damaged *gill* can kill the fish.
contrast: Almost always used in the plural: *gills*.

gloss: A long flexible arm that a sea animal uses to feel, grab, or sting.
examples: A squid has ten *tentacles*.
One *tentacle* curled around the diver's wrist.
The jellyfish's *tentacles* trailed for several feet.

gloss: A broad flat limb that a sea mammal or turtle uses to swim.
examples: The seal pushed itself along on its front *flippers*.
A turtle dug a nest with its back *flippers*.
The whale slapped the water with one huge *flipper*.

gloss: The hole on top of a whale's or dolphin's head that it breathes through.
examples: Spray shot out of the whale's *blowhole*.
Dolphins have one *blowhole*; most big whales have two.
It closes its *blowhole* before it dives.

gloss: The thick layer of fat under the skin of whales and seals.
examples: *Blubber* keeps these animals warm in freezing water.
A layer of *blubber* can be more than a foot thick.
Whale *blubber* was once boiled down for lamp oil.
contrast: Uncountable: *a lot of blubber*, never 'a blubber'.

gloss: The stiff fringed plates in some whales' mouths that strain food from water.
examples: *Baleen* works like a giant strainer.
Corsets used to be stiffened with *baleen*.
A humpback has hundreds of plates of *baleen*.

gloss: Large brown seaweed that grows in tall underwater forests.
examples: Sea otters wrap themselves in *kelp* so they don't drift away.
The *kelp* here grows two feet a day.
A storm tore loose most of the *kelp* off this point.
contrast: Uncountable: *some kelp*, not 'a kelp'.

gloss: Simple plant-like organisms that grow in water, from green film to seaweed.
examples: *Algae* had turned the whole pond bright green.
Warm water and fertilizer runoff make *algae* bloom.
He scraped the *algae* off the inside of the tank.
contrast: Used as a mass noun; the singular *alga* is almost never heard.

gloss: The tiny plants and animals that drift in the water and feed larger sea life.
examples: Whale sharks live entirely on *plankton*.
The net collected a jar of *plankton* in ten minutes.
Most of the ocean's oxygen comes from *plankton*.
contrast: Uncountable: *a lot of plankton*, never 'planktons'.

gloss: Tiny shrimp-like sea creatures that huge whales feed on in swarms.
examples: A blue whale eats several tons of *krill* a day.
The swarm of *krill* stretched for miles.
*Krill* oil is sold in every drugstore now.
contrast: No -s: *tons of krill*, never 'krills'.

gloss: Grass-like plants that grow in shallow salt water and shelter young fish.
examples: Manatees graze on *seagrass* all day long.
Boat propellers have scarred the *seagrass* in the bay.
*Seagrass* stores a surprising amount of carbon.

gloss: A ridge under the sea built up over centuries by tiny coral animals.
examples: We flew out to snorkel on the *coral reef*.
Warmer water is bleaching *coral reefs* worldwide.
A healthy *coral reef* is noisy if you listen underwater.

gloss: A long-legged bird that feeds along beaches and mudflats.
examples: Thousands of *shorebirds* stop here on their way south.
A *shorebird* ran along the waterline poking at the sand.
The refuge was set up to protect nesting *shorebirds*.

gloss: A dark diving seabird that spreads its wings out to dry after fishing.
examples: A *cormorant* sat on the piling with its wings open.
*Cormorants* can swim underwater for a surprisingly long way.
The *cormorant* came up with a fish crosswise in its beak.

gloss: A slim white seabird with a forked tail that dives straight down for fish.
examples: A *tern* hovered, then dropped into the water like a dart.
*Terns* nest right on the open sand here.
The Arctic *tern* flies from pole to pole every year.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *turn*.

gloss: A tall white wading bird with a long neck and long thin legs.
examples: A snowy *egret* stood dead still in the shallows.
*Egrets* were nearly wiped out for their feathers.
There's an *egret* in the marsh behind the house every morning.

gloss: A small brown-and-white shorebird that runs back and forth with the waves.
examples: A flock of *sandpipers* scattered as we walked up.
The *sandpiper* chased the wave out and ran back in.
*Sandpipers* probe the wet sand for tiny crabs.

gloss: A short-billed shorebird that runs a few steps, stops, and pecks.
examples: The beach is roped off to protect nesting *plovers*.
A *plover* pretended to have a broken wing to lead us away.
*Plovers* are hard to spot against the dry sand.
contrast: Rhymes with *lover*, not with *over*.

gloss: The shape of the land where it meets the sea.
examples: The *coastline* here is all rock and no beach.
Storms are reshaping *coastlines* all over the state.
We drove the whole *coastline* in two days.

gloss: The land right along the edge of the sea.
examples: We walked the *seashore* looking for shells.
The national *seashore* protects forty miles of dunes.
Her whole childhood was spent on the *seashore*.

gloss: The area next to the sea, thought of as a place to visit.
examples: They spent every August at the *seaside*.
There's a little *seaside* town about an hour north.
She misses the *seaside* more than anything.
contrast: Common in Britain; Americans usually say *the beach* or *the shore*.

gloss: The hard empty shell of a sea creature, found on the beach.
examples: She filled a bucket with *seashells*.
A pink *seashell* was half buried in the wet sand.
We glued *seashells* around the edge of the mirror.

gloss: A model castle built out of wet sand on a beach.
examples: The kids spent all afternoon on a *sandcastle*.
The tide flattened every *sandcastle* on the beach.
There's a *sandcastle* contest here in July.
contrast: The *t* in *castle* is silent: SAND-kas-ul.

gloss: The ground at the bottom of the sea.
examples: The cable runs along the *seabed* for nine hundred miles.
They mapped the *seabed* with sonar.
Something was moving on the *seabed* below us.
contrast: Normally used with *the*: *the seabed*, never 'a seabed'.

gloss: A shallow place in the sea where sand or rock rises near the surface.
examples: The chart shows a *shoal* just past the entrance.
Two boats have gone aground on that *shoal* this year.
*Shoals* shift after every big storm.
contrast: *Shoal* can also mean a group of fish, the way *school* does.

gloss: A small pool of seawater left among the rocks when the tide goes out.
examples: The kids spent an hour poking around the *tide pools*.
A *tide pool* can hold crabs, anemones, and small fish.
Go at low tide if you want to see the *tide pools*.
contrast: American *tide pool*; the British say *rock pool*.

gloss: Wood that has floated in the sea and washed up on shore.
examples: We built the fire out of *driftwood*.
A huge piece of *driftwood* was wedged in the rocks.
She makes lamps out of *driftwood*.
contrast: Uncountable: *a piece of driftwood*, never 'a driftwood'.

gloss: A pull of water back under the waves that can drag a swimmer off their feet.
examples: The *undertow* was strong enough to knock me down.
Watch the kids — there's a real *undertow* today.
A sign warned about the *undertow* near the jetty.

gloss: A narrow, fast flow of water heading straight out from the beach.
examples: If you're caught in a *rip current*, swim sideways to the beach.
*Rip currents* kill more people here than sharks ever have.
The flags mean there's a *rip current* somewhere along this stretch.

gloss: The everyday word for a strong current pulling away from shore.
examples: He got caught in a *riptide* and had to be pulled out.
*Riptides* are worst around the mouth of the inlet.
The lifeguard whistled everyone in because of the *riptide*.

gloss: A wave with a breaking white top, made by wind on open water.
examples: *Whitecaps* meant the wind had picked up.
There wasn't a single *whitecap* on the lake at dawn.
The bay was covered in *whitecaps* by noon.

gloss: A long rolling movement of the sea, without breaking waves.
examples: There's a big *swell* coming in from the storm offshore.
The boat rose and fell on the *swell*.
Surfers wait all year for *swells* like this.

gloss: A wave that curls over and breaks into white water as it reaches shore.
examples: The *breakers* were head-high all morning.
A *breaker* knocked the board out of his hands.
You could hear the *breakers* from the parking lot.

gloss: A very small wave on the surface of water.
examples: There wasn't a *ripple* on the water.
*Ripples* spread out from where the fish jumped.
A breeze put a light *ripple* across the bay.

gloss: Fine salt water blown into the air off the tops of waves.
examples: *Sea spray* had crusted the windshield with salt.
You could taste the *sea spray* on your lips.
Wind carried *sea spray* halfway up the cliff.
contrast: Uncountable: *a lot of sea spray*, never 'a sea spray'.

gloss: A long ridge of sand just under or above the water near shore.
examples: You can wade out to the *sandbar* at low tide.
The boat ran up onto a *sandbar*.
*Sandbars* move around after every hurricane.

gloss: A flat muddy area uncovered by the sea at low tide.
examples: The *mudflats* fill up with birds twice a day.
We sank to our ankles crossing the *mudflat*.
At low tide it's all *mudflats* out to the channel.

gloss: Low coastal wetland flooded by salt water at high tide.
examples: The *salt marsh* behind the dunes is full of crabs.
*Salt marshes* soak up storm surge before it hits town.
A boardwalk runs out across the *salt marsh*.

gloss: A high piece of land that sticks out into the sea.
examples: There's a lighthouse out on the *headland*.
We hiked to the *headland* to watch for whales.
Fog rolled in around the *headlands* first.

gloss: A wall built out into the sea to protect a harbor from waves.
examples: Waves exploded against the *breakwater*.
People fish off the *breakwater* all summer.
The town built a second *breakwater* after the storm.

gloss: A wall along the shore built to keep the sea from washing the land away.
examples: The *seawall* runs the whole length of the beach.
Waves came right over the *seawall*.
Rising water has cities arguing about *seawalls*.

gloss: A ring-shaped coral island with a lagoon in the middle.
examples: The plane landed on a strip of sand across the *atoll*.
Rising seas threaten low *atolls* first.
From the air the *atoll* looked like a green necklace.

gloss: A group or chain of islands.
examples: The *archipelago* has more than two hundred islands.
We sailed through the *archipelago* for a week.
Volcanic *archipelagos* form over hot spots.
contrast: The *ch* is said /k/: ar-kuh-PEL-uh-goh.

gloss: A long narrow arm of the sea between steep cliffs.
examples: The cruise took us up a *fjord* with waterfalls on both sides.
*Fjords* were carved out by glaciers.
The water in the *fjord* is hundreds of feet deep.
contrast: The *j* is said like *y*: FYORD. Sometimes spelled *fiord*.

gloss: The time when the sea is at its lowest level and the shore is uncovered.
examples: At *low tide* you can walk all the way out to the rocks.
*Low tide* is around six in the morning this week.
The boats sit on the mud at *low tide*.
contrast: Used without an article: *at low tide*, not 'at the low tide'.

gloss: The time when the sea reaches its highest level on the shore.
examples: The whole beach disappears at *high tide*.
*High tide* comes in fast here, so watch the causeway.
They timed the launch for *high tide*.
contrast: Used without an article: *at high tide*, not 'at the high tide'.

gloss: A very large destructive ocean wave that floods the shore.
examples: A *tidal wave* wiped out the whole waterfront.
He dreamed about a *tidal wave* coming over the dunes.
Scientists prefer *tsunami* to *tidal wave*.

gloss: A cool wind that blows in from the sea, usually in the afternoon.
examples: The *sea breeze* comes up right around two o'clock.
A *sea breeze* made the heat bearable.
*Sea breezes* keep this town ten degrees cooler than inland.

gloss: Salt made by letting seawater dry up.
examples: Finish the steak with a little flaky *sea salt*.
*Sea salt* costs more than table salt but tastes about the same.
The recipe calls for coarse *sea salt*.

gloss: Water containing salt, like the water of the sea.
examples: *Saltwater* rusted the hinges in a single season.
He rinsed the *saltwater* off the board.
These fish can't survive in *saltwater*.
contrast: Written as one word before a noun — *a saltwater tank* — and often as two, *salt water*, on its own.

gloss: The water of the sea, taken as a substance.
examples: The plant turns *seawater* into drinking water.
A bucket of *seawater* was sitting on the dock.
*Seawater* freezes at a lower temperature than fresh water.

gloss: Very salty water, whether from the sea or made for preserving food.
examples: The olives came packed in *brine*.
Runoff *brine* from the plant is dumped offshore.
He soaked the turkey in *brine* overnight.
contrast: Uncountable: *some brine*, never 'a brine'.

gloss: Frozen seawater that covers parts of the polar ocean.
examples: Polar bears hunt from the *sea ice*.
Summer *sea ice* has shrunk dramatically.
The ship pushed through thin *sea ice* for two days.

gloss: The line where the water reaches on a boat's hull or along the shore.
examples: The boat was loaded down past the *waterline*.
Birds were feeding right at the *waterline*.
You can see the old *waterline* on the pilings.

gloss: The animals and plants that live in the sea, taken together.
examples: The oil spill killed *sea life* for miles.
There's more *sea life* on this reef than anywhere else nearby.
The exhibit is all about *sea life* in cold water.
contrast: Uncountable: *a lot of sea life*, never 'sea lives'.

gloss: The plants and animals of the ocean, especially as a subject of study.
examples: Plastic is a growing threat to *marine life*.
She studies *marine life* in the deep ocean.
The reserve was created to protect *marine life*.
contrast: *Marine* is said muh-REEN, with the stress on the second syllable.

gloss: The nausea some people feel from the motion of a boat.
examples: *Seasickness* ruined the first day of the trip.
She takes a pill for *seasickness* before every crossing.
*Seasickness* usually passes after a day at sea.
contrast: Uncountable: *bad seasickness*, never 'a seasickness'.

gloss: Someone who catches fish, for a living or for sport.
examples: A *fisherman* was mending his net on the dock.
Local *fishermen* say the catch is down again this year.
My grandfather was a commercial *fisherman*.
contrast: Irregular plural *fishermen*, said FISH-ur-muhn — the same as the singular.

gloss: Someone who fishes with a rod and line for sport.
examples: *Anglers* line the bank every opening day.
A patient *angler* will outfish an impatient one.
The state sells about a million *angler* licenses a year.

gloss: An area or industry where fish are caught commercially.
examples: The cod *fishery* collapsed and never came back.
New rules cut the season for several *fisheries*.
This is one of the best-managed *fisheries* in the world.

gloss: The activity of catching fish.
examples: We went *fishing* off the pier at sunrise.
The *fishing* has been slow all week.
*Fishing* is closed in this stretch until June.
contrast: Uncountable: *good fishing*, never 'a fishing'.

gloss: A mesh of knotted cord used to catch fish.
examples: They hauled the *net* in hand over hand.
The *nets* came up almost empty.
He threw a cast *net* off the seawall.

gloss: A fishing boat that drags a large net behind it.
examples: A *trawler* was working the edge of the bank.
Half the *trawlers* in the fleet are tied up.
He spent three seasons on a *trawler* in the Bering Sea.

gloss: Food put on a hook or in a trap to attract fish.
examples: We stopped for gas and *bait*.
Something took the *bait* right off the hook.
Cut *bait* works better than lures out here.
contrast: Uncountable: *some bait*, never 'a bait'.

gloss: An artificial bait, usually shiny or brightly colored, tied to a fishing line.
examples: He switched to a silver *lure* and caught two right away.
His tackle box is full of *lures* he's never used.
A *lure* has to move like a wounded fish.

gloss: The rods, lines, hooks, and other gear used for fishing.
examples: All my *tackle* is in the back of the truck.
The *tackle* shop opens at five.
He bought new *tackle* for the trip.
contrast: Uncountable in fishing: *some tackle*, never 'a tackle' (a football *tackle* is countable).

gloss: A small weight tied to a fishing line to pull the bait down.
examples: Add a heavier *sinker* if the current keeps moving your bait.
The *sinker* snagged on a rock.
He keeps his *sinkers* in an old film canister.

gloss: A long spear with a rope attached, thrown or fired at large sea animals.
examples: The museum has a whaling *harpoon* on the wall.
He threw the *harpoon* from the bow.
*Harpoons* were made with a barb so they wouldn't pull free.

gloss: The fish taken on a fishing trip.
examples: They weighed the *catch* at the dock.
It was the biggest *catch* of the season.
Bad weather cut everyone's *catches* in half.

gloss: A slatted cage lowered to the seabed to catch lobsters.
examples: He pulls three hundred *lobster traps* a day.
An old *lobster trap* sat on the porch as decoration.
Each *lobster trap* is marked with a colored buoy.

gloss: A boat used to catch fish.
examples: A *fishing boat* was heading out past the breakwater.
Twenty *fishing boats* work out of this harbor.
We chartered a *fishing boat* for the afternoon.

gloss: A glass container of water where fish are kept.
examples: There's a *fish tank* in the waiting room.
The *fish tank* needs cleaning again.
He set up a saltwater *fish tank* in the basement.

gloss: A round glass bowl for keeping a pet fish.
examples: The goldfish went around and around the *fishbowl*.
A *fishbowl* is really too small for most fish.
She used an empty *fishbowl* to hold candy.

gloss: A place where fresh fish and shellfish are sold.
examples: The *fish market* opens before dawn.
We picked up two pounds of shrimp at the *fish market*.
*Fish markets* down by the harbor sell whatever came in that morning.

gloss: A place where fish are raised in pens or ponds to be sold as food.
examples: Most of the salmon in the store comes from a *fish farm*.
The *fish farm* keeps its pens a mile offshore.
*Fish farms* have been blamed for spreading disease to wild stocks.

gloss: A place where fish eggs are hatched and the young fish are raised.
examples: The *hatchery* releases half a million young salmon a year.
We toured the trout *hatchery* on a school trip.
State *hatcheries* stock these rivers every spring.

gloss: The activity of going out on a boat to see whales.
examples: We booked a *whale watching* trip out of the harbor.
*Whale watching* is best here in March.
The town makes more from *whale watching* than it ever did from whaling.
contrast: Uncountable: *go whale watching*, never 'a whale watching'.

gloss: The mass of eggs laid in water by fish or frogs.
examples: The shallows were thick with *spawn*.
*Spawn* clings to the weeds until it hatches.
Most of the *spawn* gets eaten before it ever hatches.
contrast: Uncountable: *a lot of spawn*, never 'a spawn' or 'spawns'.

gloss: The tank-and-hose equipment that lets a diver breathe underwater.
examples: He learned to dive on *scuba* at sixteen.
*Scuba* gear takes up half the trunk.
You need a certification card to rent *scuba* here.
contrast: Originally an acronym, now an ordinary word — and uncountable.

gloss: A close-fitting rubber suit that keeps a swimmer or diver warm.
examples: You'll want a *wetsuit* — that water is fifty degrees.
Her *wetsuit* was hanging over the railing to dry.
*Wetsuits* come in different thicknesses.

gloss: Someone who swims underwater, usually with breathing equipment.
examples: Two *divers* went down to check the anchor.
A *diver* found the wreck in 1987.
Commercial *divers* make good money and take real risks.

gloss: A ship destroyed at sea, or the accident that destroyed it.
examples: Divers explore the *shipwreck* every summer.
There are dozens of *shipwrecks* along this coast.
He survived a *shipwreck* off Cape Hatteras.
contrast: The *w* in *wreck* is silent: SHIP-rek.

gloss: The business of hunting whales.
examples: *Whaling* built this town in the 1800s.
Commercial *whaling* has been banned for decades.
The museum's whole second floor is about *whaling*.
contrast: Uncountable, and said just like *wailing* (crying).

gloss: Catching so many fish that the population cannot recover.
examples: *Overfishing* wiped out the cod off this coast.
Quotas were set to stop *overfishing*.
*Overfishing* is a bigger threat here than pollution.

gloss: Someone who rides ocean waves on a board.
examples: A dozen *surfers* were already out at dawn.
The *surfer* paddled over the top of the wave.
*Surfers* watch the forecast the way farmers watch the sky.

gloss: The hard shiny rainbow-colored layer inside some sea shells.
examples: The buttons are real *mother-of-pearl*.
*Mother-of-pearl* was inlaid along the neck of the guitar.
The inside of the shell glowed with *mother-of-pearl*.
contrast: Always hyphenated and uncountable: *a piece of mother-of-pearl*.

gloss: Broken glass worn smooth and frosted by years in the sea.
examples: She collects *sea glass* every time we go to the beach.
A piece of blue *sea glass* is a lucky find.
There's a jar of *sea glass* on the kitchen windowsill.
contrast: Uncountable: *a piece of sea glass*, never 'a sea glass'.

gloss: An imaginary sea creature with a woman's upper body and a fish's tail.
examples: Sailors used to claim they'd seen a *mermaid*.
She dressed as a *mermaid* for Halloween.
The fountain has two stone *mermaids* on it.

gloss: How much salt water contains.
examples: *Salinity* drops near the mouth of the river.
They measure the *salinity* of the bay every week.
Oysters can handle a wide range of *salinity*.
contrast: Uncountable: *low salinity*, never 'a salinity'.
